 Postcard from Linz: Ireland fans arrive into a city with a growing football footprint
 Updated / Friday, 13 Nov 2026
 22:15
 LASK's modern Raiffeisen Arena sits on the site of the old Linzer Stadion 
 Raf Diallo
 By Raf Diallo in Linz
 RTÉ Sport Journalist
 If there was any indication that Linz was bit of an afterthought outside of Austria's borders, a couple of anecdotal tales of Irish fans making early bookings for Vienna summed it up.
 The Republic of Ireland were drawn into the same UEFA Nations League group as Austria all the way back in February.
 A casual observer might have been forgiven for assuming that the Boys in Green's away trip would be in Vienna, a happy hunting ground ten years ago . But it wasn't until May that confirmation came that it would not be held in Austria's capital.
 While Vienna is often mentioned in the same lavish breath as the likes of Paris, Milan and Barcelona, the country's third biggest city Linz has lived in its considerable shadow internationally.
 Almost 90 minutes of a train journey from Vienna, Linz is perched up in the northern portion of Austria and has the reputation of being an industrial hub.
 But landing into its small airport, the first two words that came to mind were "bleak" and "foreboding" - not adjectives that would be in the lexicon of too many tourist boards.
 A grey pallor was the main takeaway on the short drive into Linz. But in fairness, that was almost entirely due to the thick blanket of fog and low hanging clouds that enveloped the city and reduced visibility upon arrival on Thursday afternoon. Ne'er a building could be made out in the gloom.
 Rain would soon follow to add to the desolate feel, with winter clearly setting in.
 Not so grey in the park near the stadium on Friday morning 
 If there's a reminder though that first impressions aren't everything, press conference day and the welcome sight of soft sunlight on Friday dispossessed one of any foregone conclusions.
 Anything but grey and drab, there was a lovely autumnal feel passing through the park that sits between the Raiffeisen Arena and Linz's small but colourful and charming old town on route back after hearing from Heimir Hallgrimsson and Nathan Collins in the morning's press conference .
 But among the green, red and browns of fallen leaves, one could also unmistakably make out the black and white stickers that bedecked lampposts and electrical boxes along the pavements.
 LASK fan(s) was here 
 On closer inspection, they were calling cards left by the supporters of the city's main club LASK, or Linzer Athletik-Sport-Klub to give them their full name.
 Back in the 1964-65 season, LASK left their first big footprint on the Austrian football map when they became the first club from outside Vienna to win the league. As if to reinforce a "wait ages for a bus" expression, two trophies did come at once as the club claimed the Austrian Cup in a famous double.
 Unfortunately for LASK, it wasn't the start of something. Rather the next six decades were marked by ups, downs but no silverware.
 As recently as the 2012-13 season, they found themselves forcibly demoted to the third tier after having their professional licence revoked amid financial problems.
 A LASK logo on the floor inside the Raiffeisen Arena 
 But as Celtic fans will know to their cost, LASK have very much been back in the years since. A takeover by local investors in 2013 was the spark for a resurgence nationally, which included a four-year managerial spell for current Nottingham Forest boss Oliver Glasner.
 By 2017, they were back in the Austrian Bundesliga and even started to make ripples in Europe, with Manchester United, Tottenham Hotspur, and a Liverpool side containing Caoimhin Kelleher among the sides they played host to in the Europa League between 2019 and 2023.
 The latter year was significant as it was also when the modern stadium that Ireland will play in on Saturday was opened.
 The Raiffeisen Arena on Friday morning before Ireland trained there 
 The Raiffeisen Arena is built on the site of the club's old Linzer Stadion and aside from being the base for LASK, the Austrian national team has increasingly started to use it as a home venue.
 Including Ireland's match, they will have played more 2026-27 Nations League group games in Linz than in Vienna, having also hosted Israel there in September.
 The Ireland game will be Austria's eighth home fixture in Linz since 2023 which is notable when you consider that they only appear to have played at the city's old stadium seven times between 1980 and a final friendly there in 2012.
 Linz is very much back on the football radar and the local club backed that up. For the first time since the double in 1960s, LASK did it again last season, getting their hands on both the league and cup for the first time in 61 years. Waiting for buses and all that!
 That propelled them into the Champions League qualifiers and despite losing 3-0 at Celtic Park, they hammered Martin O'Neill's Hoops 5-1 at the Raiffeisen Arena to secure Champions League football. As Ireland captain Nathan Collins jokingly responded when asked in the press conference, Liam Scales hasn't brought up that experience this week.
 Progression to the league phase has meant that Linz has become a footballing magnet with Liverpool supporters among those to have visited the city this autumn and Porto still to come in the new year.
 A slight rebrand for one establishment 
 As for Ireland supporters, one of the main sports bars in the city, the Chelsea Pub in the heart of the old town has renamed itself Jack Charlton's Pub for the week that's in it.
 Nearby on the bridge spanning the blue Danube, a small group of Irish fans kitted in green and sporting unmistakeable Donegal accents, were heading in the general direction of the old town.
 Ireland fans cross the Nibelungen Bridge with the ARS Electronica Centre in the background 
 Behind them on the far bank of the river stood the striking Ars Electronica Center which bills itself as a "Museum of the Future". Lit up in electric blue on Thursday night, in many ways it underlines the city's transformation from industrial centre to a place of modernity off - and on - the pitch.
 For Ireland fans though, the hope is that they leave Linz as satisfied as the away contingent did in Vienna when James McClean made the difference in November 2016.
